The finding

Can you tell whether a first-order logic translation says what its sentence says, without a gold formula?

Gold references for are expensive, and audits find that roughly 40% of benchmark annotations contain errors. The paper tests a gold-free alternative. Ask several independent LLM families to translate the same sentence, check with the Z3 solver which of their formulas are logically equivalent to the candidate, and score the candidate by the share of that disagree with it. That score is .

On the development set it separates faithful translations from errors better than cheap API judges: 0.741 against 0.642 for the flash-lite judge.

+0.099

AUROC gain over the disguised flash-lite judge on the population, 95% CI [+0.049, +0.146].

The answer comes with a hard caveat. Confirmation on fresh data failed: every fresh-data cell was either not testable or unfavourable. The metric also raises false alarms on meaning-preserving renames, and its power falls with sentence length. Read it as a preliminary lead.

      What the paper does not show

      • Development data only. Every positive result in the main table is on data used to design the metric. The confirmation attempt produced no testable positive cell.
      • Rename vulnerability. A 76.5% false-alarm rate on nonce renames means the metric will penalise translations with non-standard predicate names, even when they are correct.
      • Length degradation. Discrimination falls with sentence length (NET +0.356), driven by correct-translation divergence. The metric is weakest on the longest sentences, where gold-free evaluation is most needed.
      • Label dependence. All development results rest on panel labels whose agreement is imperfect; part of the advantage could reflect agreement with panel biases.
      • Cost. Cheaper than a frontier judge, but it needs k peer translations per sentence: $0.95 per 1,000 sentences at k = 3.
      • Domain. English→FOL from MALLS and ProverQA only. Other formalisms, languages and sentence distributions are untested.
